utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's have the witness brought in, please, Brigadier Marin. Good morning to everyone, good morning to the interpreters, to the Prosecution, to the Defence, and we can now, we will resume our work as soon as the Brigadier has come into the courtroom. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I hope that you've rested up a bit, that you're ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I am ready and I have rested as much as one can rest during the course of one night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right, the day is going to be long, and we hope that the Prosecutor will finish his cross-examination today. Isn't that what we hope, Mr. Kehoe? You're going to concentrate all of your efforts on that, I know you've spent the night thinking about how you're going to ask the most compact and direct questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have sleepless nights thinking about that, Judge. I will direct my attention to finishing as promptly as possible, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Judge Shahabuddeen and I would like to thank you in advance, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier, good morning, Your Honours, counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me turn your attention back to --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me turn your attention back momentarily to Exhibit 321, the map you talked about yesterday, wherein we discussed the shelling in the Vitez area. I want to ask you, sir, when the shelling was taking place in the Vitez area, were the prisoners that you discussed the day before yesterday, were those Bosnian Muslim prisoners still located in the cinema building and the basement of the cinema building some 100 metres behind the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, the prisoners were in the cinema building at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any orders to attempt to move them so they were not present when the shelling took place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I know that on that day a certain number of civilians was returned to the village of Gacice, to the best of my recollection, women and children. I'm not aware of any orders being issued in relation to that, but since I know the town of Vitez, there is not a single building where people would be safer in case of shelling than that particular building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's talk about these women and children that were taken back to Gacice. Were they in downtown Vitez before they were taken back to Gacice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The village of Gacice is right next to the town of Vitez, and as far as I know, these civilians were in town, and I cannot say what the exact location was, I cannot say it at this point. However, the town of Vitez is not a very big town, so it could have been between the post office, the municipality building, the sin man building, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these people from Gacice when they were in town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I did not see these people, because I said under what conditions I had been working. What I said just now is what I found out later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you find this out from?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that is in the report of the Vitez Brigade, too, for the day of 19th. I think that that report is attached -- rather it was tendered into evidence by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will get back to that, sir. But before we move on to that Mr. President, I would just like to bring the Court's attention to an ECMM document, unfortunately it's just in English. I might hand it out and explain some of the printing in this regard, because there was some double printing when ECMM printed it out. And Mr. President, in an effort to be expeditious we will read only two paragraphs of this document which will be the focus of our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how we have to work.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 529.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an ECMM report of 19 April 1993. I will read paragraph one, "The general situation still very tense in and around Vitez. The car bomb which exploded near the mosque in Vitez at, on 18 April, has caused great damage. Fighting with SAS, small arms and fighting with mortars and artillery still going on." We move down four paragraphs and the numerical sequence seems to be off and we go to 6, "Humanitarian. The team visited 62 male Muslim prisoners held in a prison under HVO brigade headquarters in Vitez. The prisoners were treated well although they were in a small space for such a large group. Their location formally is a violation of the Geneva Convention." Now, Mr. President, by way of explanation, the paragraphs that are crossed out are a duplication, and at the risk of going through this again, you can see this is a duplication of what is written above, sir. That is why it's crossed out. We will move down to the next page, talking about the tasks of 20 April. "The team as yesterday visited the HVO Brigade commander in Vitez and made complaints about being fired upon from confirmed HVO positions, the lifting of blockades and cease-fire on behalf of the team were arranged and seemed to be effective. The investigation of the car bomb yesterday was discussed." Now, the HVO Brigade commander on the 19th and 20th of April 1993 was Mario Cerkez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The commander of the Vitez Brigade was Mario Cerkez, if that is what was meant by this, then I can confirm it. However, HVO commander is too general a term. The commander of the Vitez Brigade was Mario Cerkez, so if this visit pertained to the visit to the Vitez Brigade, then I can confirm it, because at that time Mario was commander of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let us move on to the 20th of April and we will discuss the reports that you just mentioned concerning Gacice which were introduced during the Defence case. I am talking about the Defence Exhibit 330 and Defence Exhibit 331. So, we're moving ahead Brigadier and now we're going to talk about the 20th of April. Mr. Usher, and Mr. Dubuisson, if we could give the witness Defence Exhibit 330 and 331.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe those are the two reports that were submitted by the Defence concerning the fighting at Gacice, Brigadier. They relate to fighting on the 20th of April. Take a look at those. You can see from Exhibit 330 that at some time in the morning, it would appear, fighting is going on in Gacice, but by 1800 hours Gacice is secured; where 47 men were taken prisoner and women and children were sent home. Do you see that, sir? Just look at those two reports in conjunction and we will move through them quickly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This statement that these men and women and children were taken prisoner in Gacice, that I confirmed during my testimony during the Defence case because I had heard about it. And your question relates to document 330, but could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to place in context your statement that at Gacice there was fighting going on and Gacice and women and children were brought to downtown Vitez, and would you agree with me that based on these two documents, 330 and 331, those women and children from Gacice were brought to downtown Vitez on the 20th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Whether they were, well, that's what it says in this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, let's stay with 331. The first line of 331 says "Heavy attacks on HVO units by Muslim forces continue throughout the afternoon." Do you see that first line on Exhibit 331, the report of 20 April, 1993, at 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, it says here that the enemy, the BH army, then, attempted, on several occasions, infantry breakthroughs on lines in the Krcevine and Krizancevo Selo regions. At the moment fierce battles are being waged in the village of Bukve, Slatina, Ljubica, Stojkovici, Krizancevo Selo, Dubravica. Could you please just move? Yes, so, it's all of these places here towards Zenica. And the village of Gacice is south of the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you can step up with the pointer and just point to the villages, that will be helpful, I think, for the Court.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: All right, Mr. President, Your Honours, from the operations report of the Vitez Brigade that we received on the 20th of April at 1800 hours, the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were attacking the following places. Krizancevo Selo -- just a minute, let me orient myself. It's over here, Krcevine, Krcevine over here, then further on, Bukve, Ljubica Grobic, Poculica. Ljubija Grobic is here, Stojkovici is here, and again, from Slatina to Krcevine, on the whole, the attack of the BH army units was taking place in this region, the village of Gacice is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Brigadier, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This is the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, on the 20th there is pretty heavy fighting on that front-line area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: According to this report we can see that there was fighting, and that it was heavy fighting at that, and the commander of the Vitez Brigade is saying that there are four killed and four wounded soldiers in this fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, the ECMM reflects, this is Prosecutor's Exhibit 187, that a T 34 tank was in a position on the mountain road between Zenica and Vitez shelling HVO headquarters and the PTT building in Vitez. Was that shelling taking place and was it done in conjunction with this heavy attacks on HVO units that you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I cannot say whether the tank was shelling on the 20th, but I know that the post office was hit by a tank. But tank fire is also considered to be shelling, but I just don't know whether it was on the 20th, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, with this heavy attacks by HVO units on the 20th, along the line that you just explained, were the Muslims also shelling the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: On the 20th -- on the 20th, according to the reports that we have here, intensive -- there was no intensive shelling of Vitez on that day. If on the 20th a tank shell hit the post office, one or two, I never showed that to be intensive shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. But at some point you do recall that the post office was in fact shelled, whether it's on the 20th or some other day, at some point the post office was shelled?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I know that the post office was hit by a tank shell. That I do know. And I think that the effects of this projectile haven't been removed until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecution Exhibit 158. It should be a document that looks like this, Mr. Usher. Brigadier, let me orient you and help you out with this exhibit just a bit. This is an exhibit that has been received in evidence, and if I may, and this is based on the testimony and the photograph, point A on this photograph is the Hotel Vitez, and this is an overhead photograph. Point B is the building that we discussed previously which is the Viteska Brigade headquarters and the adjacent cinema building we can see that we talked about before. And point C would be the PTT building. I know you may not have seen this before, Brigadier, I'm just trying to orient you for a moment, and just take a second to take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I have oriented myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Now, the point number one in the circle, do you see that? There is a one over to the --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the women and children from Gacice on the 20th, did you see them taken to the location in the circle? And I'm talking about 247 women and children.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I have already said that women and children and prisoners from Gacice, that I did not see all of them, any of them. But I know that in the report we received from the Vitez Brigade I received information that these people were in town, that the women and children were returned to their homes, and that it is already the 20th of April, and there was a meeting held in Zenica, and certain activities were already taken by the commissions that are supposed to carry out this exchange of prisoners held by the Bosniak Muslim army and the prisoners held by the HVO, because already on the 20th we had a meeting in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that the, you received a report, or the headquarters received a report that the civilians were in town. That fact does not, is not reflected in either of the reports that the Defence, that you talked about during your direct examination, Exhibit 330 and Exhibit 331. Is there another report from the Vitez Brigade that reflects that these women and children were, from Gacice, were in town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I cannot recall now having received such a report, but if we look at the report that I talked about, and that arrived at 1800 hours, that report, I mean, that report put together all the activities for that day, that is to say presented all the activities for that day. At 1800 hours, to the best of my recollection, the commander, General Blaskic, had already went to the joint meeting with the representatives of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at a top military level where General Halilovic was and General Petkovic, in relation to the cease-fire, that is. The report reflects all the activities in the zone of responsibility and all the events related to the Vitez Brigade for that day, that is why the exact hour has been specified, that is to say 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for you, Brigadier, is that the fact that women and children were brought to Gacice is not reflected in Defence Exhibit 331, the report of 20 April 1993, at 1800 hours, excuse me, brought from Gacice into Vitez. The fact that women and children were brought from Gacice to Vitez is not reflected in this report. I ask to you take a look at this report once again.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: From Gacice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Your question is the fact that the women and children were taken from Gacice to Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the report it is stated quite clearly that we received the report in terms of the situation in the zone of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade at 1800 hours and it says that 40 men were taken prisoner and that the women and children were taken home. I do not know the exact time when they were taken home and I don't know the exact time when they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Brigadier, and all I'm asking you is, is there another report from the Viteska Brigade that you received in the headquarters telling you that these women and children had been taken from Gacice to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Now I cannot remember that kind of report. If I were to see it and to see its contents, when I see the document, I mean, I remember the contents, especially if these are contents of such a nature. Taking a target, heavy fighting, then my memory is jogged and then I can discuss such matters. But if I were to claim now that there was some kind of report or there was not some kind of a report, it would not be objective on my part. But to the best of my recollection, there was not. Because this report is not an extraordinary report, it is the regular report that we have been receiving in terms of the regular reporting during fighting and combat action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, from Exhibit 331, the report that is before you, you can conclude two things, or at least one thing, that throughout the afternoon, heavy fighting is taking place with Muslim forces, and you told us that prior to 1800 hours, women and children from Gacice were in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it does say here in the report. Heavy fighting, heavy fighting in the places that I mentioned, and I'm going to repeat these locations Krcevine, Krizancevo Selo, that was infantry fighting, and these locations are 3 or 4 kilometres away from the town of Vitez, and that is fighting between two armies that are entrenched. That is to say, the HVO on one side and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other side and that is the fighting that is referred to in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe, let's not go around and round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, on the 20th of April did any member of the HVO come into the Hotel Vitez and tell you or Colonel Blaskic or any other officer in the headquarters that women and children were outside the Hotel Vitez at this location that is circled in Exhibit 158, the one that's on the ELMO? Did any soldier do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but I know that out of those civilians who were brought in, none were killed and none were wounded that day. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you told us that this meeting, excuse me, this report of 1800, Exhibit 331, was issued at 1800 hours after the women and children were sent home. What time did Blaskic go to this meeting in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I know General Blaskic set out for Zenica between 17 and 1800 hours, I cannot state exactly when. As far as I know the meeting was supposed to be held around 1900 hours, but specifically what I know for sure is the following: That the meeting was on the 20th, the time I cannot confirm. From Vitez to Zenica in war time conditions, one needs one hour to get there by vehicle, so that time can be specified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let's go back to this Exhibit 331, where the Viteska Brigade says women and children were sent home. Brigadier, what happened to those women and children?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I know they were sent home. They stayed there in their village. I know that after the fighting that took place in the village of Gacice the HVO took control over the village of Gacice. The members of the units of the BH army were driven out of the village. I do not know of the fate of these people afterwards, but if they had not stayed on in the village of Gacice through the work of the commissions, I assume that these same people moved out under the organisation of UNPROFOR. They went to the area either of Zenica or some other town. I do not have accurate information as to whether some of these families stayed on in the village of Gacice during 1993. But what I do know is that in a certain number of houses in the village of Gacice where Muslim Bosniaks had lived until then, Croats, refugees from Zenica and other places, moved into these houses. During the fighting between the BH army units and the HVO units, if there was such fighting, then the Croats would move out, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, were you present in the headquarters when any member of any humanitarian aid organisation came to talk to Colonel Blaskic about the fate of the women and children in Gacice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, as regards my activity, from the 16th until the 25th, I was in the operation centre all the time. The representatives of international organisations did not come to this operation centre. The office of the commander was further away, and it had a special entrance, a separate entrance, and whether they came to see General Blaskic, that I cannot confirm. For me, when I got this report from the Vitez Brigade, the most important thing was that none of these civilians were killed and that the women and children were sent home. In view of my responsibility, that was a job that was finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I'm not limiting your time to simply the 25th of April. I'm talking about the period of time that takes us into, say, the first or second week in May. From the time these people were taken from Gacice to Vitez and back to Gacice on the 20th, until, say, the second week in May, were you aware of any international humanitarian organisation coming to the Hotel Vitez to talk to Blaskic about the fate of these women and children that were in Gacice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Exactly as to that question I am not aware that anybody came. But after the 20th, and after the meeting in Zenica that already at that time a cease-fire had been defined and a cease-fire agreement had been signed, and within that framework of those activities, an in exchange of prisoners was decided upon, the Croats taken by the BH army and the Bosniak Muslims taken by the HVO. So this business of the 20th was taken over by commissions and they were headed by the civilian authorities of the Muslim Bosniaks, and so on. Now, under what circumstances when and how they performed this exchange, I cannot tell you in detail at the moment and give you the facts of those exchanges, but I know that it was under competency of those commissions and that the work was finished. That is to say, after the duty had been executed, the exchange commissions had exchanged all the prisoners and nobody stayed in prisons, both the Croats taken by the Muslim Bosniaks and vice verse a. That's what I know about that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, how far is Gacice away from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Gacice is, according to my assessment, one and a half to two kilometres away from the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, were you aware, or do you know if Blaskic was aware, that in the early part of May of 1993 HVO soldiers came to this village, picked these women and children up, put them on trucks and took them to the road going to Zenica where they were told to walk across the front-lines? Were you aware of that? You were the chief of operations at the time. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was chief of operations, but I'm not aware of that fact. And it is not my business to deal with civilians, women and children as chief of operations. From the meeting in Zenica and from the meeting on the 21st in Bila, everything concerning prisoners, civilian prisoners, was under the charge of the commission coordinated and headed by the civilian authorities, the representatives of the Croats in Vitez and the representatives of the Bosniaks in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, if you were chief of operations during that period of time, isn't it your job to know virtually everything that is going on in the headquarters when it comes to Blaskic's orders and meetings and exactly what HVO forces are doing? Isn't that your job?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is my job, and I do know that. I know that Blaskic went to Zenica, that a commission was sent up following orders and that they dovetailed their opinions and did these activities with the refugees and that the assignment was completed. Whether this was done in one day, two days, three days, and the problems that arose, who made the problems, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it also your job, Brigadier, to know that HVO soldiers, under the command of Colonel Blaskic, are putting civilians on trucks and taking them to the mountain road? Isn't that part of your job to know those things?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: It is if I get information of this kind, then quite normally I would react as the commander, and I would write a document, but I had no information of that kind. And I repeat, all concern about the refugees was taken over by the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a follow-up question on that, Brigadier, and we will end with this area. Isn't it true that into May the Muslim houses in Gacice that were a kilometre or so away from the headquarters, isn't it true that those Bosnian Muslim houses were burnt?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as the burning of houses in the village of Gacice is concerned, there was burning, both in the course of the fighting and there was burning after the fighting. I spoke of this burning and under what circumstances it took place. There were both Croatian and Bosnian houses burned in Gacice. The consequences of these burning, after the conflict and after the cease-fire had been signed, I went into that matter yesterday, and I explained it yet and I don't want to tire the judges with those facts. I said that the reasons were that if one Croat house was burnt, by the Bosnian side, then it was not excluded that somebody would in retaliation burn two or five Muslim houses. So that the burning of houses was a problem throughout 1993 in Central Bosnia, it was a problem that we in the command and in the Operative Zone had to fight against. And we had orders expressly forbidding this. But it was done secretly, and you could never arrive at a name. I will tell you of one example. After the fighting in Krizancevo Selo, when the BH army in one night in an attack killed 70 members of the HVO, including civilians, ten houses were burned in Grbavica, straight away. So, this is cause and effect, and I condemn that. But, that is the tragedy of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, by early May of 1993, as chief of operations, you knew that there were no Muslims left in the village of Gacice; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Up to the beginning of May, I did not know whether all the Muslims within the exchange plan had been, had left Gacice or whether somebody had remained living in Gacice. I cannot ascertain that, maintain that. The region under my control, I did not only have the village of Gacice, I had 50 other similar villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Brigadier, but by early May virtually every Muslim was gone from the village of Gacice; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I cannot say that that is so, but I believe that it was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask anybody where they went?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I said that through the exchanges of individuals, those who were taken prisoner had the possibility of going home or to have UNPROFOR enable them to go to another locality; however, people, both Croats and Bosnians, because of the situation that reigned, that is to say, a situation of war, usually opted for going to those places and those settlements which were controlled by their own army. The Croats came to places under HVO control and the Muslim Bosniaks went to the places controlled by the BH army. The other reason was that after the conflict and the units had been driven out, the HVO was in control and the soldiers had been expelled, then their families would go with them, and that took place on the other side, as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let's switch subjects. Now, Brigadier, we talked previously in an exhibit that we chatted about yesterday or the day before, and I'm referring to Exhibit 514, which is an English ECMM report of the 6th of February, 1993, where trench digging was taking place, or Muslim labour was used to dig HVO trenches in the Busovaca area. Now, sir, let me ask you a question. During this time frame, did you have information that the -- we don't need to go into it. We don't need to refer to the document. That's okay. We just want to use that as a reference point to move on. During the time frame of April of 1993, did you receive information that Croats, Bosnian Croats were taken prisoner in the village of Poculica, and that Bosnian Croats were forced to dig trenches for the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Could you tell me the report in question? Because at this particular moment I cannot recall a report with that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, candidly, Brigadier, I'm reading the opening statement of Mr. Hayman, which is at page 11.217, and he stated that on the morning of the 16th of April in Poculica, what happened. It was a mixed village of Muslims and Croats. More Muslims than Croats, and on the morning of the 16th --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Units in Poculica attacked the Croat part of the village, hundreds of Croats fled into a stream to try to escape down the hill, and approximately 70 did not flee, and they were captured by the territorial Defence forces in Poculica. In the following days, regrettably these detainees were taken in groups to dig trenches, some were forced to go into no man's land to collect bodies while tethered to a rope which their captors held on to. And, indeed, a number of them were murdered and wounded by shooting incidents involving a HVO soldier." Do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps for clarity in the interpretation it was the Croats who were taken prisoner, not Muslims taken. It was -- we're dealing with Croats, and I don't think it was quite clear in the interpretation. So, we're talking about the Croats taken prisoner by the territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I thought perhaps there might be a difference of interpretation as regards all these words from the Defence. Would you make the correction Mr. Kehoe so that the question is clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Defence counsel is a hundred per cent correct, this incident refers to Bosnian Croats being taken prisoner and forced to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It wasn't that clear. I thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: When we're talking about the place of Poculica, where the mixed population, Croats and Muslims, that is to say that after the conflicts, as the Croats lived there, there was the HVO, and the Bosnians suppressed Croats from that village. I did not see Croats digging trenches, I did not see them, but as I know what the situation was like, it is possible, although I cannot claim that that was so, because I did not see it take place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Brigadier, that you didn't see it taking place. My question is, did you hear about this incident taking place in the Hotel Vitez? Did this information come to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I don't recall any information of that kind. But, because of the overall situation, as a result of the conflict, it is possible that it was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear information in April that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was forcing Bosnian Croats to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This kind of information most often could be heard, so, if you didn't get a report from your own unit, information of this kind could be heard through the public media, public information media. And so, this kind of information was put out, used by the media for propaganda purposes. So that when you hear this kind of information over the radio, whether it was the Bosnian Muslim radio or Croatian radio station, as a soldier, I never took it to be one hundred per cent true, I always had some reservations with regard to that information. So, I know it was possible, but I cannot claim that it was actually so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let's talk about a couple of exhibits, based on what you just talked about and what you heard and what you thought was possible, and what you heard on the radio. If I can take in series, Defence Exhibit 298 and Defence Exhibit 314, and then if I could have -- use in that sequence, and then Defence Exhibit 301, and Defence Exhibit 325. So the sequence I would like to follow is Defence 298, 314, 301 and 325. Brigadier, the Defence Exhibit 298 is an order that you drafted on the 17th of April, 1993 at 2000 hours, going to all these units and special purpose units, signed by Colonel Blaskic, and on number 4 of that particular order, the order is to dig in on the front-lines and prepare a counter-attack. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in response to your order, let us turn to Exhibit 314. This is a response that comes from the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade. Their response is on 18 April 1993, and it notes that it is a report on the implementation of your order, the order that we just discussed in 398, the order in April of 323, and it says in response, among other things, it says in point 4, "Entrenchment has been carried out on all defence lines in order to organise the defence from the enemy as efficiently as possible." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. It is in document 314, is it not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct, Brigadier. Now, we're talking about digging trenches here; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In document 298, point 4, it states that entrenchment has been carried out in all defence lines in order to organise the defence for the enemy as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kehoe. Let me look at Mr. Fourmy, because he speaks both languages. When you say in French “retranchements", that could mean something else than WHAT is indicated here as "entrenchment". Can that mean, in French, digging trenches, "retranchements"? Because frequently it means that you're, it is a rather ambiguous term. That is what is said. All right. But it can also mean digging trenches. Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we're talking about here, Brigadier, is the digging of trenches. When you ordered the digging in on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Entrenchment on the front-lines incorporates the following: digging trenches, that is to say digging trenches for the activity of the soldiers, and entrenchment, depending on the situation, and we say in military terminology, of the traffic lines, communication lines. So, communication lines or communicating trenches, so that these trenches are linked up, and the defence can be a good quality defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to Defence Exhibit 301, which, again, is an order that was written by you, again on the 17th of April, 1993, but this is going to the Viteska Brigade personally. Do you have that before you, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it, and I remember the contents of that order. I think that I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that your initials on the left-hand corner and I think you're correct.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you talked about this on your testimony in direct about the sectors, et cetera, and on number 3 you order the Viteska Brigade to carry out first level engineering work in the sectors, to dig standing trenches, and the deadline is 0500 hours on the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, and that is quite normal when an order of this kind is given, because you cannot defend yourself unless you have entrenched. That is a military operation that takes place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while the next exhibit, 325, while not a direct response to that order, there is a response on the digging of trenches by the Viteska Brigade, and I'm talking about the response on 19 April, 1993 at 0600 hours. On the third paragraph down, it says, "Further mobilisation of personnel has been carried out, and new trenches and reinforcements are continuously being created on all defence lines." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, and that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these trenches were being dug all along the line in the sectors that you have described in Defence Exhibit 301; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is, in all the sectors on all the defence lines, and all the villages. That is to say, all the Croatian villages, trenches in front of the Croatian villages to enable the villages to defend themselves with respect to the BH army units on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this trench digging, Brigadier, this is very dangerous work; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Every combat operation is dangerous, and that includes trench digging. There is nothing in wartime that is not dangerous, and trench digging is, of course, a dangerous job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trench digging -- you would agree with me, would you not, Brigadier, that trench digging is particularly dangerous, because you're digging the trenches on the front-line in front of the enemy; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. It would not be professional of me to say that it is not dangerous to be at the front-line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the sectors that you are -- let me -- the sectors that you are describing in Exhibit 301, in the order to the Viteska Brigade, those sectors are mostly in the Vitez municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, let me clarify that, why the order came into being. When we spoke about the establishment of the Vitez Brigade, we saw how far it had been organised and set up. And on the 17th, when we concluded, the force that the BH army had to launch an attack, and that we were threatened by this danger, that is to say, the danger that the BH army would repulse the forces from the Vitez Brigade. At that point we decided, and in view of the existing set-up, to link up one village and the other village, and a third village, and then we could say that is sector one. Then one village and another village and say that is the second sector. So, we have that degree of establishment where we did not have any companies, or battalions or anything else. So, this was seen to be a good solution for those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, according to the testimony of Brigadier Ivica Zeko, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had 82 to 84.000 soldiers, while the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, had 8.000 to 8.200, and the question to Mr. Zeko by Mr. Nobilo, on page 11.717, Mr. Nobilo asks Brigadier Zeko, “So if we could simplify the proportion, it would be ten to one in favour of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and Brigadier Zeko said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Let me just add, so that we don't have any dilemmas, the 8.000 figure or whatever you said, is how many soldiers we had carrying arms. That is soldiers ready for combat. Whereas we had on our lists about 13.000 soldiers but without arms. But what we could have used, that is to say soldiers equipped with weapons, was the figure that you mentioned, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's again turn our attention back to the Defence Exhibit 345, and if we could keep these exhibits up -- if we could keep those exhibits handy. You don't have it right now, Brigadier. We'll get it for you. Now, this is, again, the document that we discussed previously about the HVO dead in Vitez during the combat time in Vitez in 1993 and 1994. If I may, Mr. President, and we can expedite matters and you can go through it at your leisure, but I think we covered the amount of dead through the 19th, but the 20th reflects two HVO soldiers killed, according to this list, and I can point them out to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, according to the list that we have, from the 16th to the 20th, while all this fighting and all this trench digging is going on, we have approximately a dozen HVO soldiers killed in Vitez, according to the list of 345, and we can go through the numbers again, if you would like. Now, this is a time when extensive trench digging has been ordered . You maintain there are extensive offences going on by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We ordered that the defence lines had to be entrenched, and towards that aim mobilisation was a work duty and civilian defence as well, and all the population that did not have weapons went to dig trenches together with the soldiers. That was the situation. There was no other solution. So we had both civilian protection and the defence, and they were work units. And the mobilisation, the department in charge, was the Defence Department for matters of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is also a time where you were outmanned, according to the testimony of Brigadier Ivica Zeko, ten to one. Now, my question for you, Brigadier, is: During this time, all this extensive activity, did you question why the HVO took so few casualties while they were performing such dangerous work in the front-lines and also in combat?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I know that there were more casualties, but in the time before us we will probably prove that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question for you is: Given all these dangerous activities, the offensives, the fact you were outmanned ten to one, all this trench digging going on, did you ask yourself, Brigadier, why the HVO is taking so few casualties, or did you know the reason why?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness said that there were more than 12 casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That point was answered, Mr. Kehoe. He said there were very few casualties, and he thought that there were others and he hoped they would be able to show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me put an exhibit on the ELMO, and this is Prosecution exhibit 263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would the witness say whether these other casualties are also indicated in this list?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, just a moment, please. I'm going to look at papers I have on the persons who were killed. It is true that these members of the HVO in Vitez were killed in the time of the war with the army of the Republika Srpska and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and 657 persons were killed. That is the exact figure. And 624 soldiers were wounded, and 140 civilians were wounded. When those two are put together that is 764. In order to understand how great this tragedy was, this should be compared to the number of 12.690 Croats who lived in Vitez. And if we compare these population figures to the fact that the war practically lasted for one year, it turns out that about 60 people were killed every month, or wounded every month, too. This list that I confirmed reflects the number of members of HVO who were killed. Civilians are not shown here. So, 657 and 624, that is the difference between civilians and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, as Honourable Judge Shahabuddeen has put this question, I feel duty bound to say a few words about this. It is not our duty to intervene and we wanted to clarify matters during our rebuttal; however, since this question was put by the Court, I think that now we are duty bound too. I think that the Prosecutor is misleading the witness. On the first page it doesn't say that this is the date of killing. He is looking at the dates that are in this column and it doesn't say that that was the date of death at all. We didn't want to stop the Prosecutor, because we have been listen being to "two or three dead" every day, day-in day-out, and we are going to give our own proof, but at this stage I think that I had to intervene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the date that's in the second column? The 1st is Rajanovic (phoen). He was born in 1970. 25 October is it? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, on the document it says nothing. It just says the date. We are going to add evidence that is going to show that this was the date of burial. Nobody could bury their dead on the 16th and 17th, because burials took place after the war had stopped. I'm talking about the column where it says the date. First is the surname, the father's name, and the name. Then the year, that is the year of birth of the person killed, and after that is the date. That is the date of burial. But it doesn't say so on the text. It doesn't say what date it is. We are going to prove that that is the date of burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The next to the last column, is that -- when you look at 12th, Bobic. If I read 1976, I thought that he was killed on the 17th of February, 1994, in Krcevine, and that he was buried in Krcevine the next day, 18 February, 1994. Is that not correct? Buried at -- let me ask for some help here. Doesn't that mean buried on the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The place of burial. It doesn't say the date of burial. May I clarify this a bit further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is a date, Mr. Nobilo, next to it. Look at number 1. Let's go back to number 1, because that was a Muslim HVO member. All right, sir, everybody should agree about this. Ianovic (phoen) was -- first column was the year, 1970. That was his date of birth. The second column, the 25th, 1973, I think that must have been the date he was killed. The place is the place where he was killed, his address and then he gives the original address, and I think that he was buried in Kruscica on the 25th of October and that's the same day, which is not illogical. It could be interpreted that way. At least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest the following; that you look at point 322. That is one example, and I have many of them. Zoran Vidovic, it says that on the 21st of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, if you're saying that, probably because it fits in with what you want to say. All right. Mirko Valenta, he was born in 1960. According to me, he was killed -- 322.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Two, Zoran Ivica Vidovic, that is 322. Vidovic, father's name Ivica, name Zoran.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 322. All right. Yes, Vidovic. Yes, I see. That's another chart, isn't it? Vidovic. At least I think he was killed on the 21st of April, 1993. We know that he was buried in Kruscica, although we don't have the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have here the official certificate from the Register of the Dead in the municipality of Vitez. This is an official document kept under the municipality. That is the beginning and the end of human life on the basis of law. There are certificates of birth and certificates of death. And Zoran Vidovic was killed on the 16th of April, the 16th of April, 1993. And this document is the one that is registered by those who are bound by law to register deaths and births, and there are many of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, let's be careful here. This is a list. This list was given to us by you. It is D345. This shows the list of the members of the HVO who were killed. When I read a date, I have a tendency to think maybe I'm wrong, but I would assume that that's the date that they were killed. At least that's what I think. All right. Perhaps we shouldn't go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know how this was written, but this is conducted by an organisation for which it is important to know how many people were killed, because of pensions, et cetera. However, the date of death is registered here, according to law, by the official authorities. So, this is exact. These are the exact dates. But, if we look at these certificates, the figures are quite different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Nobilo. Let me remind you this is a clarification which you must provide for your own document, because originally it was your document. This is why we have to start with that document now. Of course, you are free to bring in any other clarifications that you want, that is your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President. We used this document in order to prove the number of dead. We did not look at the dates. When the Prosecutor picked this up, then we tried to get authentic documents which prove otherwise. We just wanted to show the proportions of death in Vitez, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It's now 20 after 11.00. Do you have another question to ask about that specific issue of dates, or do you want to change subject? What do you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't have any particular question about the dates of this, Mr. President, and we will continue on in this area, but there are quite a few questions in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right then. We're going to take a break, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are you going to use all these documents, or can we put them away now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to use them any more, Judge, we can put those away. I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you said earlier this morning that you had heard on the radio, both on the Muslim radio and the Croat radio, that civilians were being used or being forced to dig trenches. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did say it, but not as you just said it. That is to say that on the radio information could be heard linked to all the activities. And if the BH army was on the air, then they would say what negative things were being done. If it was the Croatian radio, they would say what negativity existed in the BH army's actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic hear those radio reports, as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I suppose that he did. And as far as I recall, that is to say, after all the events, when General Blaskic completed all his knowledge and the problems that were happening, occurring on the terrain, he issued an order in which he expressly said how soldiers should conduct themselves, and all the negative features that he had been informed of, to prevent this from happening, to stop it from happening. And that in the units, in town, that is to say, where soldiers were moving about, that conduct should be carried out in a soldierly fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, are you saying that Blaskic learned that HVO soldiers were forcing Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I believe that in talks with international organisations, in talks at meetings with the representatives of the BH army, that such matters were also discussed because this was happening on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, was any member of the HVO arrested for forcing a Bosnian Muslim to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Digging trenches, that is to say engaging people in entrenchment, in entrenching the defence lines, and fortification, which means the digging of trenches, the digging of communications trenches, the digging of shelters for people to hide from in the rain and in the night, so that kind of activity was performed by the soldiers within the framework of their work assignments where necessary, and people from the units, and from the Civil Defence units and the other population, if this was necessary at any particular location. I cannot say that in the village of Krcevine there were 10 or 15, but, Mr. President, for an overall picture of the state of affairs to be gained, I should like to indicate on the map where these defence lines were and where the digging and entrenchment and fortification took place. The dugouts, and the communicating trenches and all the other work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is that really necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, what is your answer to the Prosecutor's question as to whether any HVO soldier was ever arrested for forcing people to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I do not know that a soldier was ever arrested. Can I show this on the map? It will be brief. Mr. President, the defence lines taken over by the HVO after the attack by the BH army went right past the villages, along the Croatian villages. Now, what do we have on the terrain? For example, your house is here, and ten metres in front is a trench, and you and your family and your children live in that house. Now, why am I saying this? I don't want to you look at this like a front-line, a military front-line, that is to say that you are taking people from here, some 50 kilometres into the mountains to dig trenches, no. Take the village of Krcevine. Who dug trenches most often there? The soldiers from that particular village, the villagers of the village, the locals. And if some devices or equipment had been mobilised, that is what trench digging meant, because the entire line in Vitez stretched between the villages, at the edges of the villages, or sometimes through the village itself, because the defence lines between the HVO units and the Bosnian units were sometimes 50 metres apart, because it was a fight for each inch of land. And that is what the actual picture with regard to trench digging was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, could on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just move the ELMO back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you were a prosecutor in the military disciplinary courts in Vitez. Do you know of any member of the HVO who was disciplined for forcing Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I was the deputy prosecutor for disciplinary matters. This disciplinary court in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, as far as I know, was established in September or October of 1993, and from that time on this disciplinary court moved certain motions and cases against officers and non-commissioned officers, but not soldiers. The disciplinary court that you mentioned was not able to pitch disciplinary -- on the discipline measures on soldiers that you're talking about, and I said I did not know that the commander of any unit disciplined a soldier, that is to say that he took him in -- he was taken into custody for activities related to trench digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any soldier in the HVO who was discharged from service for forcing Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches, anyone?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: At that particular time it was not possible to discharge anybody from service because nobody was in the service. But I do know when it happened in Busovaca, in Kaonik, that some -- and we did have an order there that General Blaskic, the commander, had ordered, and this was the military police that carried this out, something with the prisoners, detainees, that an order was issued that this should be ascertained, why this had been done, who had done it and under what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, that was in February, that order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in February. You're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about in April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December, January, December of '93; January, February, March of '94. Name me one HVO soldier who was disciplined, discharged or prosecuted by the military prosecutor for forcing a Bosnian Muslim to dig trenches. Name me one.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I cannot claim that this was done with any soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 263. Mr. Usher, if we could put this on the ELMO. Brigadier, this is a photograph of an individual who has been identified as Zlatko Aleksovski who was the warden of the military prison at Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, this is Zlatko Aleksovski on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read to you, sir -- and I am referring to exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 242, and this is attached Annex O to Prosecutor's Exhibit 242, dated the 10th of May, 1993. And in a conversation with a monitor for the ECMM, Zlatko Aleksovski said the following -- he was talking about prisons and the problems in the prison in Busovaca: "The Fifth problem" -- and I'm referring to page 2 of the document. "The Fifth problem is the kind of work that the prisoners have to do, because I know that the Geneva Conventions do not allow prisoners to be taken away for any work if their lives are in danger. I have been warned about that by the ICRC, as well. But I am not the only one responsible for this, because I just carry out orders. The brigade commanders in Busovaca and Vitez give them. Not that I want to avoid my responsibility, because I am the one who releases people to do the work. In order to clear it up, I went with Beatrice, of the ICRC, to the commander in Busovaca, where she protested for the people to be taken to work under such conditions. She was given the answer I almost completely agree with. We here actually do not have enough people to do the security jobs. Someone had to dig the trenches, and it happened that the men to do that were the prisoners." Brigadier, did you know that Bosnian Muslim prisoners were taken from the military prison camp in Busovaca, that they were taken there by the brigade commanders in Vitez and Busovaca and taken to dig trenches? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: This fact, the fact that you repeated and that you stated here is not something that I was aware of. But later on I learnt of these events, that they did take place, and from April, further on, as far as I remember, the commander of the Operative Zone did issue a command that such things should not be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the two brigades that we discussed previously that orders were given to dig trenches were the Viteska Brigade and the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: We're dealing with those two brigades, but those brigades were not responsible over -- of control over the military prison camp, just as the commander of the Operative Zone. The military prison in Busovaca was under the Ministry of Jurisdiction, and the area where this military prison camp was located, as far as I know, it was an area where the prisoners were detained. How long, how many of them and under which conditions, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there has been a misinterpretation. He said that the military prison in Busovaca was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice and it said "jurisdiction". It was the Ministry of Justice, not "jurisdiction".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's been noted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, we have established previously in a Blaskic order, have we not, that Blaskic gave a direct order to the warden of all military prisons in June of 1993 forbidding taking prisoners to dig trenches. So on at least one occasion on a Defence exhibit -- and I can show you that exhibit, if you want. On one occasion, in a Defence exhibit, Blaskic is forbidding the warden to allow prisoners to dig trenches; isn't that right? Or would you like to see that document again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, show the document again, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's Defence Exhibit 373, the order of 21 June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to take the time. Brigadier, I'm going to ask you once again to try to remember that you were the chief, the number two person of military operations. You're trying to create -- it was a question of creating defence lines. Show the document to the witness again. I know we're wasting time, but too bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a direct order of Colonel Blaskic. INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a direct order from Colonel Blaskic to the brigade commanders and to the wardens of the military prisons, 21 June, 1993, and number 2, forbidding using prisoners of war to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. This order was given to the commanders of the brigade to implement. It was sent to the warden of the military prisons, because certain soldiers, independently, came to the warden of the prison and wanted to take people away. Therefore, the wardens were -- said that -- he can say, "General Blaskic sent an order that this was forbidden and I cannot allow to you do this. " That is how I understand this order, and I know the order was issued for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Kehoe, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again on point 4, Blaskic holds the warden of the military prison responsible for carrying out this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. Hayman. I see you're making certain gestures. It's your witness's answer which makes the Prosecutor say what he says, because suddenly he’s answering about competence. He said -- Mr. Nobilo had the transcript corrected. He said that the prisons were under the authority of the ministry. Therefore, it is legitimate on the Prosecutor's part to bring in this document. The document has to be seen with a certain cohesiveness in the totality. It is a question of legal logic, Mr. Hayman. The Prosecutor has to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. I'm not being to the line of questioning. I'm objecting that we had this same line two or three days ago. I'm just objecting to the repetition, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's true, but you have to admit, Mr. Hayman, it is extremely difficult -- at least for this judge speaking to you right now, I'm not speaking for my colleague, it's difficult to find the cohesive and logical line within the witness's testimony. You have this kind of a question which causes a problem, because it is -- there is an exculpatory document here, you yourself presented it. But if it is exculpatory, then of course the Prosecutor wants to see the total cohesiveness of the document. You used -- and now he is trying to use it for a question -- in a question which seems legitimate to me. Mr. Kehoe, ask your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the person who was running the prison in -- the military prison in Busovaca is Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes. He was the warden of the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is the one that's saying that brigade commanders in Busovaca and Vitez are taking prisoners out to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I heard that from your report, the one you read out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, is forcing Bosnian Muslim prisoners -- is forcing Bosnian Muslim prisoners to dig trenches a violation of the Geneva Convention or is it a war crime?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, forcing any civilians to dig trenches is not in line with the Geneva Conventions, and that is what it says in this order of ours, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn that prisoners, Bosnian Muslim prisoners, were being forced to dig trenches? When did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I really cannot tell the exact date and time, but since such orders were issued, I knew that such incidents did occur, and the reaction of the command of the Operative Zone was to try to stop this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this same line, it's true, is it not, that members of the ICRC came to the Hotel Vitez and met with Colonel Blaskic and protested using Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether they came with that question in mind. I know that international organisations, throughout the year, came to see the commander of the Operative Zone. I can only confirm and speak of the things we did and the certain documents we made to resolve certain problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I just want to note an objection, Mr. President. The Prosecutor, it appears, is stalling so he doesn't have to finish his cross today by 1.30. He is asking the exact same questions, exact same questions we heard two and three days ago, and we object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm trying to move through this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Kehoe, continue in this area. This is a witness that you called in, who is the number two operational man who was involved with organising defence lines. And the defence lines, I'm not saying that they -- they could be a probability, that civilian prisoners dug the trenches. I think in all the briefings in the mornings they must have spoken about the organisations of the defence lines, and I regret, Mr. Hayman, for the time being, the judge speaking to you has not yet heard the answer from the number two person in the headquarters of the accused. Please continue and we will continue on the 26th if necessary. Mr. Kehoe, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, as the chief of operations and when you were the deputy commander, did Blaskic go to the prison at Kaonik, the military prison at Kaonik to determine for himself whether or not Bosnian Muslim prisoners were being taken out to dig trenches? Did he do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, whether the General did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the headquarters in Vitez? And I'm saying did you stay in there into 1994, were you still serving in September, and October and November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: In 1993, yes. Yes, I was, until the Washington Accords. And then in March 1995, I was transferred to another duty in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you an exhibit which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 448, if I may, Mr. Dubuisson, which is a photograph that looks like this. Now, Brigadier, take a look at the three orange circled areas, and I want to focus on the areas over to the right. The areas on the right include the area known as Bobasi, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, Bobasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in September, October and November there was a lot of fighting in the Bobasi area, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September, through to November, where -- by the way, before I ask that question, how far is Bobasi from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Between two-and-a-half and three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was testimony before this court that Bosnian Muslims, from September through to November, were being forced to dig trenches in the areas circled in orange, which includes Bobasi. My question for you, Brigadier, as the chief of operations at the time, did you know that Bosnian Muslim males were being taken up to the Bobasi area and forced to dig trenches, on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I am not aware of that as concerns Bobasi. I know that the soldiers who were up there and the duty platoons that already existed attached to units, they were digging trenches up there. But in September?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, are you telling us that you know units were digging trenches, but you know nothing about Bosnian Muslim males being forced to dig trenches? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: The trenches were dug by soldiers from the units that were there, and they were dug by work platoons that were established and were attached to the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Brigadier, we will move on to another subject at this point. I want to talk to you, Brigadier, about some of your testimony about Colonel Blaskic when he received information of a crime or information of an event. You testified about how he acted promptly on complete and timely information. Let me just give you a small sampling of some of the items you commented on, the first being on page 12.551. You said that, “Whenever General Blaskic had complete and timely information about an event, he would react immediately, so as to deal with the problem." On page 12.561, you note that talking about an exhibit that confirms that the information came to reach General Blaskic in a timely fashion, and he took steps to resolve it. 12.566, he -- again commenting that Blaskic, when he received information in a timely fashion, he would take immediate steps. And the last one I will reference you to is 12.374, "General Blaskic, whenever he had the opportunity and had timely information, did not wait one second or one minute, he would take measures immediately" -- excuse me, “he would take action immediately and take measures to solve the problem." Now, you also told us, Brigadier -- and I will show you the Defence Exhibit in mind, if I can, Defence Exhibit 379. Now, Defence Exhibit 379, you noted that this was not a full report, yet you noted in your testimony that Colonel Blaskic acted on it, even though it was not full and complete information. And this relates to the destruction of the mosque in Kiseljak, and I refer you to your testimony on 12.615.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Blaskic, according to your testimony, reacts immediately with timely information that he receives, and even in this instance where he doesn't have complete information, you maintain that he responded to it. Now, let me ask you some preliminary questions about the period of time on the 16th. You were getting a significant amount of information, according to your testimony, from civilians who were calling into the Hotel Vitez about shooting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, the Defence would like us to move into closed session now, because we believe that for the reasons we mentioned earlier, we are now getting to that date, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I don't have any objection. I certainly don't want to do anything to jeopardise the Brigadier. If something comes out at this point, I guess it's better to be safe at this point, if it doesn't, we can take care of releasing this testimony down the line, or portions of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will move into a closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session) (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, we're going to finish today at 5.45, therefore, compact your question, concentrate them, focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm trying, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And I'm sure that the witness will do the same for his answers. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to inform the Defence that I signed the order calling the witness in again. Brigadier, I ask that you try to answer as concisely as you can when the questions are asked so that we can finish with the cross-examination by 5.45 today.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: I shall do everything in my power, Mr. President, to be as precise as possible, but the questions, however, dictate the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, Your Honours. If the Brigadier could be given 335, Defence Exhibit 335 again, Mr. Usher. This is the document we were talking about just before lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, I think you stated -- INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this document, Exhibit 335, after Blaskic returned from the meeting in Zenica, whether it was on the 20th or the 21st, this report is the 21st, he told you about the tragedy in Ahmici; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, we confirmed this on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Brigadier, so, he knew at that time that HVO soldiers had been involved in a terrible event that took place in Ahmici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Yes, he had information on that, that is, that the killing of civilians had taken place and that a large number of houses had been burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he also knew that HVO soldiers were involved.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN
utterances.text: Nobody else could have participated by the HVO soldiers, so he knew it was the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, let me direct your attention, I will read this, and this is a Prosecution Exhibit 184, which is a report by the commission on human rights, Mr. President, that is in both French and English. Now, Blaskic told an investigator for the United Nations Commission on human rights on about the 5th of May of 1993, he denied, adamantly denied allegations that HVO soldiers carried out such attacks around Vitez, including Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Misquoting the testimony of the Mr. Akhavan, Your Honours. Could we have a quote please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure, I'll gladly give you a quote. Quote, this page 5.297. First of all, I was quoting the report, but I'll gladly quote the transcript as well and this is the transcript of Mr. Payam Akhavan. "Colonel Blaskic did not deny that atrocities had been committed in Ahmici, but he did not try to persuade me that these atrocities had not occurred, but he adamantly denied that any of his soldiers would have been involved in such an operation. I repeated once again, that all evidence linked HVO soldiers to that attack and he repeated his position, that as far as he was concerned, none of his soldiers would have committed such atrocities."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President, he said they were not my soldiers and that is what counsel has quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
